summary: Defines the base syntax for Certificate Management over CMS (CMC), a protocol for requesting and managing public key certificates. It provides an interface to certification services built on CMS and PKCS #10 and an enrollment protocol that can be used with those. It updated an earlier CMC specification and was later replaced by RFC 10002.

plainLanguage.summary: CMC is the wire format for asking a certification authority for a certificate. The request bundles together the certification request itself, a set of numbered instructions called controls, and any extra CMS messages, then wraps the lot in a signed or authenticated envelope. The answer comes back in the same shape, with a status code saying whether the request succeeded, failed or is still waiting.

how does proof of possession work in cmc
subtitle: The message format a client and server use to ask for a certificate and to answer.

tldr.problem: The world of public key certification already had building blocks: CMS for signing and encrypting, PKCS #10 for asking for a certificate. There was no agreed way to combine them into one request that could also carry proof of identity, proof of possession and everything else a certification authority needs.
tldr.mechanism: CMC defines two request forms and two response forms, built out of CMS SignedData and AuthenticatedData objects. A request carries a list of controls, each a numbered tag plus its data, alongside one or more certification requests.
tldr.outcome: A client can get a certificate in a single round trip, and the server can say precisely what went wrong. The document was updated by RFC 6402 and later obsoleted by RFC 10002.

today: RFC 5272 was published in June 2008 as a Proposed Standard. It was updated by RFC 6402 and has since been obsoleted by RFC 10002. It had itself obsoleted RFC 2797.

sections.title: What CMC Is For
sections.content:
The RFC defines the base syntax for CMC, a certificate management protocol built on the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). It addresses two needs inside the Internet public key infrastructure community: the need for an interface to certification products and services based on CMS and PKCS #10, and the need for an enrollment protocol for encryption-only keys, where the algorithm or the hardware makes signing with the key impossible.

A small number of additional services supplement the core certification request service. The requirements the protocol sets for itself are worth reading as a list of design constraints: it must build on the existing CMS, PKCS #10 and CRMF specifications as much as possible; it must support the current industry practice of a PKCS #10 request answered by a PKCS #7 certs-only response as a subset; it must easily support the multi-key enrollment protocols required by S/MIME and other groups; it must supply a way of doing all enrollment operations in a single round-trip, and when that is impossible the number of round-trips must be minimised; it must be designed so that all key generation can occur on the client; support must exist for the mandatory algorithms used by S/MIME; it must contain proof-of-possession methods; it must support deferred and pending responses for cases where external procedures are required to issue a certificate; and it must support arbitrary chains of Registration Authorities between the requester and the Certification Authority.

The document was reorganised from its predecessor RFC 2797. Information about how to transport the messages was moved to a separate document, and information about which controls must be implemented and which algorithms are required was moved to a second one, so that this document with those two forms a full definition.
sections.plainLanguage: CMC fills a gap between pieces that already existed. There was a standard way to sign and encrypt a message, and a standard way to ask for a certificate, but no agreed way to put them together in one request that also proves who is asking. The RFC also lists what it expects of itself, such as finishing in one round trip wherever possible and letting the client generate its own keys.

sections.title: Two Requests, Two Responses
sections.content:
A PKI enrollment transaction is generally a single round trip: a PKI Request goes from the client to the server and a PKI Response comes back. When certificate issuance is delayed, more than one round trip is needed. The RFC defines two request types and two response types.

A Simple PKI Request is a bare PKCS #10 certification request, used when no other service is needed. It must not be used when a proof of identity has to be included, it cannot be used when the private key cannot produce a signature of some kind, and it cannot be used for any of the advanced services the document defines. The Full PKI Request is one or more PKCS #10, CRMF or other request structures wrapped in a CMS encapsulation as part of a PKIData. A Simple PKI Response is a certs-only SignedData, and a Full PKI Response is a PKIResponse content type wrapped in a SignedData. When a Simple PKI Request succeeds the answer is a Simple PKI Response; when it fails the answer is a Full PKI Response, and the server may choose to return nothing at all.

Renewal, where a new certificate uses the same key, and rekey, where a new certificate uses a new key, get no special services. They look like any other certification request, except that the identity proof comes from an existing certificate issued by a trusted certification authority.

Registration Authorities may sit between the end entity and the certification authority. To the end entity an RA looks like the certification authority, and to the server the RA looks like a client. An RA can batch several requests together, perform the challenge and response proof of possession itself, add private or standard extensions to every request, archive private key material, or route requests to different certification authorities. When it forwards a request it may forward it unchanged, add a new wrapping layer, or remove existing layers and add a new one. It must not alter any certification request, because altering one would invalidate the signature on it and with it the proof that the client holds the private key.

The specification makes no assumption about the transport. The use of CMS does not imply email, and several transports are defined in a companion document. The optional services are transaction management, replay detection through nonces, deferred certificate issuance, revocation requests, and retrieval of certificates and certificate revocation lists.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a minimal form and a full form of both the request and the answer. The minimal request is the plain certificate request that everyone already used. The full form adds a set of numbered controls so the server can also be told to prove identity, to return extra data, to batch requests, and so on.

sections.title: The Shape of a Full Request
sections.content:
The Full PKI Request is encapsulated in either a SignedData or an AuthenticatedData whose encapsulated content type is id-cct-PKIData, identified as {id-pkix id-cct(12) 2}. The PKIData structure is a sequence of four parts: a control sequence of tagged attributes, a request sequence of tagged requests, a CMS sequence of tagged CMS objects, and a sequence of other messages.

The control sequence holds the controls defined in the document; controls may also be defined by other parties. The request sequence holds the certification requests, each of which may be a PKCS #10 CertificationRequest, a CRMF CertReqMsg, or an externally defined request. If an externally defined request is present and the server does not understand it or will not process it, a status of noSupport must be returned for that request and no other certification request is processed. The CMS sequence holds CMS message objects. The other message sequence holds arbitrary data objects, which are referred to by one or more controls; this lets a control refer to a large amount of data without the data being embedded in the control itself.

All certification requests encoded into a single PKIData should be for the same identity. When SignedData is used, the signature may be made with the private key of an embedded signature certification request or with a previously certified signature key. When the key of an embedded request is used, that request must include a Subject Key Identifier extension, the subjectKeyIdentifier form of the signer identifier must be used in the SignerInfo, its value must be the Subject Key Identifier from the request, and there must be only one SignerInfo. When AuthenticatedData is used, the Password Recipient Info option must be used, a randomly generated key computes the message authentication code over the content, and the key derivation input is the concatenation of the identifier encoded as UTF-8 and the shared secret.
sections.plainLanguage: The full request is one of the standard CMS envelopes with a PKIData block inside it. That block has four slots: the numbered instructions, the certificate requests, other CMS messages, and arbitrary data that the instructions can point at. Keeping large data outside the instructions lets one instruction refer to a lot of data without carrying it twice.

sections.title: Controls: The Numbered Instructions
sections.content:
Controls are carried in both Full PKI Requests and Responses. Each one is encoded as a unique object identifier followed by the data for that control. A processing system detects the identifier first and processes the corresponding value before it processes the message body. All the identifiers sit under the arc id-cmc, which is itself under id-pkix.

The document defines thirty of them. The status controls report how a request or response turned out: the Extended CMC Status Info control is preferred and the older CMC Status Info control is kept for compatibility with RFC 2797, and a server may emit several status controls for one body part. The status value is a number: success means the request was granted or the action completed, failed means it was not and more detail is elsewhere in the response, pending means the request has not been processed and the requester must poll back, noSupport means the operation is not supported, confirmRequired means a Confirm Certificate Acceptance control must come back before the certificate can be used, popRequired means a direct proof of possession is required, and partial means only part of the response is being returned and the requester must poll for the rest.

When something fails, a CMCFailInfo value gives the detail: badAlg for an unrecognised or unsupported algorithm, badMessageCheck for a failed integrity check, badRequest for a transaction that was not permitted, badTime for a message time field too far from the system clock, badCertId when no certificate matches the criteria, unsupportedExt when a requested X.509 extension is not supported, mustArchiveKeys when the private key material must be supplied, badIdentity when the identification control failed to verify, popRequired and popFailed for proof of possession, noKeyReuse when policy forbids reusing a key, internalCAError for an unknown internal failure, tryLater when the server is not accepting requests at that moment, and authDataFail when processing authenticated data failed.
sections.plainLanguage: A control is a numbered instruction attached to a request or an answer. The number tells the server what kind of instruction it is, so the server can act on it before it reads the rest of the message. The status controls say how things went, with a list of specific failure reasons such as the identity check failing or the server being busy.

sections.title: Proving Identity and Proving Possession
sections.content:
Some certification authorities require a proof of identity in the request. CMC provides one based on a secret shared between the client and the server, and clients that support the Full PKI Request must implement it. The proof starts with an out-of-band transfer of a token, which should be generated randomly and whose distribution is out of scope. The client then computes a hash of the shared secret as a UTF-8 string using the named hash algorithm, computes a message authentication code over the encoded request sequence using that hash as the key, and puts the result in the witness field of the Identity Proof Version 2 control. The server recomputes the same value and compares it. A failure to verify must be reported with the failure code badIdentity. Implementations must support tokens of at least 16 characters. The older Identity Proof control is processed the same way, but with the hash fixed to SHA-1 and the MAC fixed to HMAC-SHA1.

An optional Identification control is a simple way for a client to say who it is, so the server can find the right shared secret. When it is present, the key is derived from the hash of the shared secret concatenated with the identity value instead of from the shared secret alone.

Proof of possession is a different thing: it shows that the client holds the private key matching the public key it wants certified. The RFC lists five forms. A signature provides it by signing some data. A direct proof uses an encrypted challenge and response. An indirect proof returns the issued certificate in an encrypted state, and is not used by CMC. A publish proof hands the private key to the issuer, and is not currently used by CMC but would be used by key generation or key escrow extensions. An attested proof has a trusted entity assert that one of the others has been done.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different things have to be shown. The client has to show it is who it claims to be, which CMC does with a secret both sides share: the client signs the request with a key derived from that secret. And the client has to show it holds the private key it wants certified, which is usually done by signing something with that key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mechanisms for thwarting replay attacks may be needed depending on the operational environment. Where the certification authority keeps significant state, replay attacks may be detectable without the optional nonce controls, so implementers need to consider their environment before deciding whether to use the senderNonce and recipientNonce controls. Developers of state-constrained PKI clients are strongly encouraged to use them.

Extreme care is needed when archiving a signing key, because whoever holds the archived key may be able to use it to generate forged signatures. There are still reasons to archive a signing key: an archived certification authority signing key can be recovered if a disaster stops the authority producing revocation lists. Care is also needed before archiving, because an archiving entity could use the keys in a way that does not suit it, and users should be made especially aware that proper verification is made of the certificate used to encrypt the private key material.

Clients and servers need to check cryptographic parameters before issuing certificates, to make sure that weak parameters are not used. The RFC points at the small subgroup attack and at methods of avoiding it, and says that CMC implementations ought to be aware of this attack when doing parameter validation.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things need care. A replayed request could be answered again with a fresh certificate, so the protocol has optional nonces for that. And a signing key that is archived to recover from a disaster is a key that somebody else may be able to use to forge signatures, so it must be handled carefully.

viz.caption: THE FOUR MESSAGE FORMS DEFINED BY CMC

cells: A bare PKCS #10 certification request, used when no other service is needed.
One or more PKCS #10, CRMF or other requests wrapped in a CMS encapsulation as part of a PKIData.
A certs-only CMS SignedData with no SignerInfo, holding the issued certificates.
A PKIResponse content type wrapped in a SignedData, with controls and other messages.
